content: Some pregnant women with diabetes are advised to express and store colostrum before giving birth. After delivery, the stored colostrum can be fed to the newborn to reduce the need for artificial formula or intravenous dextrose if the baby experiences hypoglycemia. However, observational studies have indicated that expressing breast milk during pregnancy might lead to earlier onset of labor and an increased likelihood of the newborn being admitted to special care nurseries for hypoglycemia management. The objective of this review was to assess both the potential benefits and risks associated with antenatal breast milk expression and storage in late pregnancy among women with diabetes. A comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of June 30, 2014. The review included all randomized controlled trials, both published and unpublished, that compared antenatal breast milk expression with no expression in pregnant women with either pre-existing or gestational diabetes and carrying a single fetus. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies identified through the search. No randomized controlled trials, either published or unpublished, were found that directly compared antenatal breast milk expression with no expression. However, one randomized trial on this topic is currently in progress. The authors concluded that there is no high-quality systematic evidence available to determine the safety or effectiveness of expressing and storing breast milk during pregnancy.
